part.text:
The anchoring-disabled test failed: `regex.test("abc999xyz")` returned true. Why? Because without anchors, the pattern can match a substring "99" or "9" etc. Indeed rangeToRegex(1,100) unanchored contains alternatives that match a substring of 999. E.g., "[0-9]" matches "9" within "abc999xyz". So unanchored regex will match any string containing a digit. My test expectation was wrong. Unanchored regex is meant to be embedded with your own surrounding pattern, not to reject arbitrary surrounding text. Let me fix the test.

Actually the anchors option is a bit odd. But it's fine. Let me adjust the test: unanchored should match "42" inside "abc42xyz"? still digits inside. Actually unanchored "42" is covered. But "abc999xyz" also matches because of a single digit. So the correct assertion: unanchored regex has no ^ $, i.e. its source doesn't start with ^. Let me test that instead.

Let me rewrite that test.

Done. Project set up with all 7 tests passing.

```
package.json              # ESM, node --test, bin entry
src/range-to-regex.js     # rangeToRegex, parseRange, rangeToRegexFromString
bin/range-to-regex.js     # CLI: range-to-regex 1-100
test/range-to-regex.test.js
```

Usage:

```bash
npm test
node bin/range-to-regex.js 1-100
# ^(?:[1-9]|(?:1[0-9]|[2-8][0-9]|9[0-9])|100)$
```

The implementation splits the range by digit length, recurses on shared prefixes, and emits alternations for the low/middle/high spans, so it also supports multi-digit, single-value, and BigInt-sized ranges. Out-of-range values with leading zeros (e.g. `007`) are rejected.
